ease off: become less strong, painful or intense
typical: rain/pain/pressure eases off. NOT for: stopping completely and suddenly.
The rain eased off in the afternoon.
The pain eased off after I took the tablet.
do something with less effort or force
typical: ease off (on) sth, ease off the accelerator. NOT for: starting with more energy.
The coach told them to ease off before the match.
Ease off a little, you're working too hard.
ease up: become less severe or less busy
typical: traffic/pressure/work eases up. NOT for: ending suddenly.
Work should ease up after the holidays.
The traffic eased up once we left the city.
relax and be less strict or less hard on someone
typical: ease up on sb/sth, e.g. ease up on the kids. NOT for: working harder.
You need to ease up on yourself a bit.
The boss eased up on the rules in summer.
eat out: have a meal in a restaurant instead of at home
typical: eat out tonight, we eat out a lot. NOT for: taking food home (use takeaway).
It's cheaper to cook at home than to eat out.
eat up: eat all the food you have been given
typical: eat up, eat sth up; often said to children. NOT for: eating only a little.
Eat up, your dinner is getting cold.
She ate all her vegetables up.
use a lot of time, money or energy
typical: eat up sth, e.g. rent eats up my wages. NOT for: food.
Rent eats up half of my salary.
The project ate up all our free time.
egg on: encourage someone to do something, usually something foolish or risky
typical: egg sb on, often about bad behaviour. NOT for: giving kind support (use encourage).
The other boys egged him on to jump from the wall.
She wouldn't have done it if her friends hadn't egged her on.
end in: have a particular result at the end
typical: end in tears/failure/a draw. NOT for: finishing at a certain time (use end at).
The match ended in a draw.
finish with a particular letter or sound
typical: words ending in -ly. NOT for: the result of an event.
Words that end in a vowel are easy to link.
end up: finally be in a place or situation, often without planning it
typical: end up in Rome, end up paying/working. NOT for: finishing something on purpose (use finish).
We got lost and ended up in a different town.
He ended up paying for everyone.
become something in the end, often by surprise
typical: end up as/with sth. NOT for: ending a meeting or event.
She started as a nurse and ended up as the hospital director.
We ended up with three cats.
enter into: begin or become involved in a discussion, agreement or relationship
typical: enter into talks/an agreement/a contract. NOT for: going into a room (use enter).
The two companies entered into a partnership.
I don't want to enter into an argument about money.
be a part of a situation or a thing to consider
typical: usually negative, e.g. money doesn't enter into it. NOT for: a physical movement.
Money doesn't enter into it; I just want to help.
Luck never entered into her success.
even out: typical: prices/the score even out. NOT for: becoming bigger.
Prices usually even out after the holiday season.
Over a year, the costs even out.
typical: even sth out, e.g. even out the surface. NOT for: making a difference bigger.
Use a knife to even out the cream on the cake.
The new tax is meant to even out differences in income.
even so: introduces something that is true in spite of what you have just said
typical: spoken and informal writing, at the start of a sentence or after 'but'. NOT for: 'even though' before a clause or 'even if' for imagined situations.
The test was difficult. Even so, most students passed.
He apologised. Even so, she was still angry.
The hotel had no sea view, but even so we enjoyed the stay.
